regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 55.9","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY is the headline; the quality check is less flattering. IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity confirm the investment leg is real — but core sector slipped to 4.8% YoY from 5.0%, and PMI composite at 55.9 is services-led, not manufacturing-led. Invert: if private capex is genuinely accelerating, why is core sector — the physical backbone of infrastructure — decelerating? The answer is that government capex is doing the heavy lifting, and private investment is still waiting for demand signals that PV sales at 7.9% YoY (falling two consecutive months) are not yet providing.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 5.54% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"Headline CPI at 5.54% YoY masks a dangerous composition: fuel at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile, 18-month high) is the accelerant, food at 7.74% YoY is the kindling, and core CPI at 3.9% YoY is the only comfort. The gap between headline and core — 164 bps — tells you this is a supply shock, not demand-driven inflation. The second-order problem: WPI at 9.92% YoY is already feeding into producer margins, and Brent rising five consecutive months to $111.86/bbl means the fuel component has no near-term ceiling. RBI's own inflation forecast of 5.1% YoY is already stale.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.4% YoY; CD ratio 81%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 19.4% YoY against deposit growth at 17.8% YoY sounds manageable at 160 bps divergence — until you note that services credit is running at 24.3% YoY and vehicle loans at 19.7% YoY, both accelerating. The CD ratio at 81% (73rd percentile) has eased from 83% but remains structurally elevated; the last time it sustained above 80% with repo at 5.25% p.a., the system needed macro-prudential intervention within four quarters. NBFC credit at 15.8% YoY (rising two consecutive months) is the pressure valve — if deposit competition intensifies, NBFCs face a funding squeeze before banks do.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. on extended pause while CPI prints 5.54% YoY means the real rate is barely positive at 29 bps — insufficient to anchor inflation expectations when fuel is at a 10-year-high percentile. The RBI's dilemma is structural: cutting would widen the India-US rate differential (US 10Y at 4.98% yield, Fed funds at 3.75% p.a.) and accelerate FII outflows already running at ₹49,935 cr / month net outflow; holding risks embedding inflation expectations. The policy rate is doing nothing for housing affordability — home loan rates at 7.35% p.a. with CPI at 5.54% YoY leaves a real mortgage rate of under 200 bps, historically insufficient to cool credit demand.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (up from 16.1%) and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile, 18-month high) are the two most credible signals of a genuine investment upcycle. The inversion: capacity utilisation above 75% is historically the threshold at which private capex decisions get made — we are through it. But core sector at 4.8% YoY (decelerating) is the contradicting signal; cement and steel dispatch, the physical proxies for construction investment, are not keeping pace with the IIP capital goods print. The upcycle is real but narrower than the headline suggests — machinery and equipment, not broad infrastructure.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹203521 cr/mo; PV 7.9% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹2,03,521 cr / month (73rd percentile) is the formalization story, not a pure demand story — the prior month was ₹1,99,853 cr, suggesting the sequential uptick is real but modest. The vehicle sales decomposition is the tell: two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY (rural proxy) are surging while PV sales at 7.9% YoY (urban discretionary) are falling for two consecutive months and CV sales at 12.6% YoY are also decelerating. This is the classic India dual-economy signal — rural demand recovering (possibly aided by a good kharif season) while urban mass-market consumption softens under fuel price pressure. The consumption regime is not neutral; it is bifurcating.","badge_label":"Stable Consumption","badge_type":"b-neu"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.4% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 17.8% YoY — a 160 bps divergence widening for 2 consecutive months (17.1% → 19.4% credit; 9.9% → 17.8% deposits). CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits, down from 82.2% but still at 73rd percentile historically. NBFC credit accelerating at 15.8% YoY (up from 10% YoY), now at 57th percentile.","implication":"RBI will face pressure to tighten liquidity or signal rate cuts to ease deposit mobilisation. Banks with CASA ratios > 45% will outperform; avoid NBFCs with wholesale funding > 30% of liabilities. Overweight private banks with strong deposit franchises (HDFC Bank, Kotak). Underweight mid-tier NBFCs reliant on bond markets — corporate bond issuance at ₹18,700 cr / month is at 0th percentile (new data point, no historical anchor).","pct_10y":73,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 73rd percentile is elevated but not crisis-level. Historically, ratios above 85% preceded NBFC stress (2018–19); current 81% is manageable if deposit growth re-accelerates.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Upcycle Firmly Entrenched","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (latest, up from 16.1% YoY), at 52nd percentile. PMI Manufacturing at 55.1 index (up from 52.8), at 75th percentile; PMI Services at 55.2 index (up from 54.1), at 84th percentile.","implication":"Capex cycle is self-reinforcing: high capacity utilisation → pricing power → investment. Equity MF net inflows at ₹38,307 cr / month (latest, up from ₹29,329 cr / month), at 80th percentile.","implication":"SIP inflows are genuine and accelerating, but average ticket size is rising (SIP AUM growing faster than account count suggests affluent money entering, not mass retail). DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile) is offsetting FII outflows (₹49,935 cr / month net outflow, 17th percentile). Domestic support is strong but fragile if equity markets correct >10%.","pct_10y":93,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 93rd percentile are at all-time highs. signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation Spike Threatens RBI Credibility","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (latest, up from 20.05% YoY), at 95th percentile — highest in 18 months. Brent crude at $111.86 / bbl (latest), rising 5 consecutive months ($110 → $110.1 → $110.7 → $111.2 → $112.3 → $113.4 / bbl). WTI at $102.35 / bbl (latest), up 4 of last 5 months. Headline CPI at 5.54% YoY (latest, up from 4.83% YoY), at 52nd percentile. Food inflation at 7.74% YoY (latest, up from 5.97% YoY), at 57th percentile.","implication":"RBI's inflation forecast of 5.1% YoY is at risk of being breached if oil stays above $110 / bbl. Overweight energy stocks (ONGC, Reliance) and underweight consumer staples with thin margins.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is a structural risk. Oil above $110 / bbl typically persists 6–9 months, adding 150–200 bps to headline CPI. Last time fuel inflation was this high (2022), RBI hiked 190 bps in 5 months.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"BOJ Tightening Unwinds Carry Trades","data_text":"BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (latest, up from 1% p.a.), at 100th percentile — highest in cycle, rising 2 consecutive months (0.75% → 1% → 1.25% p.a.). Fed funds rate at 3.75% p.a. (latest, up from 3.63% p.a.), at 68th percentile, rising 2 in a row. US 10Y Treasury yield at 4.98% yield (latest, down from 5.05% yield), at 90th percentile. ECB deposit rate at 2.5% p.a. (latest, up from 2.25% p.a.), at 63rd percentile, rising 2 in a row. US PMI Composite at 58.4 index (latest, up from 56 index), at 91st percentile.","implication":"BOJ tightening is the tail risk. Yen carry trades (borrow JPY at 1.25%, invest in INR/USD at 95.24 ₹ / USD) are unwinding — this explains INR weakness and FII outflows (₹49,935 cr / month net outflow). If BOJ hikes to 1.5% p.a. in next 2 months, expect 200–300 bps INR depreciation and $2–3 bn FII outflow. Reduce leverage; hedge USD exposure. Overweight INR-hedged dollar assets (US equities via ADRs, US Treasuries). Avoid carry trades in emerging markets.","pct_10y":100,"pct_note":"BOJ at 100th percentile is unprecedented in this cycle. Historically, BOJ tightening cycles last 12–18 months and trigger 15–25% yen appreciation, unwinding $50+ bn in carry trades globally.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Weakness Signals RBI Intervention Limits","data_text":"INR at 95.24 ₹ / USD (latest, up from 94.94 ₹ / USD), at 89th percentile — strong-negative signal, rising 2 of last 5 months (96.15 → 97.09 → 96.15 → 95.24 → 94.34 → 95.24 ₹ / USD). FII equity net at ₹49,935 cr / month net outflow (latest, 17th percentile). DXY at 101.961 index (latest), at 55th percentile, rising 3 of last 5 months. Overweight INR-denominated assets (government securities, bank deposits) and underweight USD-exposed corporates (IT services, pharma). Hedge INR exposure via forwards or options.","pct_10y":89,"pct_note":"INR at 89th percentile weakness is a structural signal of capital outflows. Historically, INR weakness above 95 ₹ / USD preceded 6–12 months of RBI rate cuts (2018–19, 2022–23).","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Rents Spike While Absorption Collapses","data_text":"Office absorption at 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter (latest, up from 17.4 mn sq ft / quarter), at 13th percentile — strong-negative signal, score -74. Yet office rents in Bengaluru at ₹168 ₹/sqft/mo (latest, up from ₹150 ₹/sqft/mo), at 98th percentile — strong-positive signal, score +96. Mumbai office rents at ₹343 ₹/sqft/mo (latest, up from ₹330 ₹/sqft/mo), at 100th percentile — strong-positive signal, score +100. Office vacancy at 13% vacant (latest, down from 15% vacant), at 33rd percentile. Nifty IT (proxy for traditional IT services) at 23,053.1 index (latest), at 74th percentile — flat, no momentum.","implication":"This is a GCC (Global Capability Centre) story, not an IT services story. Absorption is rising because multinational tech firms (Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Apple) are expanding GCCs in India, not because Infosys/TCS/Wipro are hiring. GCCs pay 30–40% higher rents than traditional IT services and occupy premium Grade-A space. Traditional IT services are stagnant (Nifty IT flat), but commercial real estate is decoupling upward. Implication: (1) Overweight commercial real estate REITs (Embassy, Mindspace) — they're capturing GCC demand, not IT services demand. (2) Underweight traditional IT services stocks — they're not the growth driver anymore. (3) Watch for GCC employment data (not yet published) — if GCC headcount grows 20%+ YoY while IT services grow 5%, this confirms the thesis. Falsification: if office absorption falls below 15 mn sq ft / quarter for 2 consecutive quarters, GCC expansion is slowing.","pct_10y":13,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 13th percentile is historically weak, but rents at 98–100th percentile is a contradiction that signals supply-demand mismatch. This divergence preceded 18–24 months of Grade-A space scarcity and 15–20% rent growth (2015–17 cycle).","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

7.8% GDP, But Urban Consumption Fading at the Edges

The facts:

  • GDP at 7.8% YoY (64th percentile) with PMI Composite at 55.9 (85th percentile) — the headline is unambiguous expansion.
  • But PV sales at 7.9% YoY are falling two consecutive months, and CV sales at 12.6% YoY are decelerating — urban discretionary and freight demand are softening.
  • Two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY diverge sharply upward — rural demand is recovering while urban mass-market weakens.
  • Core sector at 4.8% YoY (down from 5.0%) contradicts IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY — machinery is being ordered; physical infrastructure output is not keeping pace.

The tension: GDP and PMI signal broad expansion, but the consumption decomposition reveals a bifurcation: rural recovering, urban softening — and core sector deceleration suggests the investment upcycle is narrower than IIP capital goods implies.

Bottom line: Watch PV sales in the next print; a third consecutive monthly deceleration would confirm urban demand fatigue and pressure consumption-facing earnings.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

Synchronised Tightening — BOJ at 100th Percentile, Fed Still Climbing

The facts:

  • BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, rising two consecutive months from 0.75%) — the most aggressive end of its decade-long range, unwinding yen carry trades globally.
  • Fed funds at 3.75% p.a. (68th percentile, rising two in a row) with US 10Y at 4.98% yield (90th percentile) — real tightening is embedded in the long end.
  • US PMI Composite at 58.4 (91st percentile) and GDP SAAR at 3.4% SAAR (rising three consecutive quarters) — US re-acceleration is genuine, which removes any near-term Fed pivot.
  • But Eurozone CPI at 3.8% YoY (rising two in a row) with ECB at 2.5% p.a. (rising two in a row) — Europe is tightening into a 1.2% YoY GDP print, a fragile combination.

The tension: Global central banks are tightening simultaneously — BOJ at cycle highs, Fed still rising, ECB accelerating — while only the US has the growth to absorb it. For EM, this is the worst configuration: dollar strength, carry unwind, and no DM growth dividend to offset outflows.

Bottom line: BOJ at 1.25% p.a. is the underpriced tail risk for India liquidity; the next 25 bps move there triggers yen carry unwind that hits FII positioning in Indian equities within 30–60 days.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

SIP Record Masks NFO Collapse — Retail Depth Without Breadth

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (93rd percentile) — rising three consecutive months, the structural bedrock of domestic equity liquidity.
  • But NFO collections at ₹998 cr / month (2nd percentile, 10-year low) — retail appetite for new product is absent; money is flowing to existing schemes, not new risk.
  • DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile) is absorbing FII equity net outflows of ₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile) — a near-perfect offset, but DII firepower depends on SIP continuity.
  • MF AUM at ₹82.64 lakh cr is down from ₹87.08 lakh cr — market-to-market erosion is shrinking the base even as flows hold.

The tension: SIP flows are record-high but YoY growth has decelerated to 10.7% YoY (30th percentile) — the absolute level is strong, but the momentum is fading. If FII outflows persist and SIP growth slows further, DII absorption capacity narrows.

Bottom line: SIP YoY growth below 10% would signal the domestic liquidity buffer is thinning; watch the November SIP print as the threshold.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

NRI Demand Holds Premium; REITs Price the Wrong Office Story

The facts:

  • NRI buying is RISING — NRI share of residential purchases at 20% (up 2 pp), with 25% share within premium/luxury; remittances at $144.8 bn (16.2% YoY) provide the funding runway.
  • Hyderabad leads city momentum: sales +15% YoY, launches +120% YoY, only 28 months unsold inventory — but the launch surge risks oversupply within six quarters.
  • Office absorption at 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter (13th percentile) is GCC-led (41% of occupier mix) — IT services at 22% is structurally shrinking its footprint, which Nifty IT at 23,053 (74th percentile, flat) has not yet priced.
  • But Embassy REIT at ₹370, Mindspace at ₹345, Brookfield at ₹263 — all down 10–28% from prior prints — while Mumbai rents hit ₹343/sqft/mo (100th percentile): the income is there, the unit price is not following.

The tension: Office rents at all-time highs in Mumbai and Bengaluru should be REIT-positive; REIT unit prices are falling because the market is discounting the IT services vacancy risk and the high-rate environment compressing yield spreads.

Bottom line: REITs become a buy when US 10Y drops below 4.5% yield — until then, the yield spread compression argument does not close.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Four Fuses, One Detonator — Crude Is the Common Thread

The facts:

  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) with Brent rising five consecutive months to $111.86/bbl — every additional $10/bbl adds ~$15 bn to India's annual import bill and widens CAD by ~40 bps.
  • FII equity net outflow at ₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile) with INR at 95.24 ₹/USD (89th percentile) — sustained outflows at this pace test RBI's intervention capacity within two quarters.
  • CD ratio at 81% (73rd percentile) with NBFC credit at 15.8% YoY rising — if deposit competition forces up term deposit rates by 50 bps, NBFC funding costs spike and credit growth stalls abruptly.
  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile) — the next hike triggers yen carry unwind; historical episodes suggest EM equity outflows of 3–5% of market cap within 60 days.

The tension: All four risks share a common amplifier: Brent above $115/bbl simultaneously widens CAD, pressures INR, forces RBI to hold rates longer, and tightens the funding environment for NBFCs — a cascade the base case does not price.

Bottom line: Watch Brent this week: a close above $115/bbl would trigger the CAD-INR-NBFC cascade and force a reassessment of the RBI pause narrative.

"}
